title: Your case preparation checklist
subtitle: Print this page. Keep it beside the case as you prepare, and bring it with your notes.

items.text: Read your instructor's questions and instructions. Use them to focus your preparation.
Preview the opening, ending, headings, and exhibits. Then read the case. Note who is involved, what is at stake, and why action may be needed.
Are you choosing an action, explaining a problem, or judging a result? Write the question your analysis needs to answer.
Study the passages and exhibits that answer your question, one issue at a time. Separate facts from interpretations and assumptions. Look for evidence against your first view.
Use a relevant concept, theory, or framework to explain the evidence. Show how it helps and where it falls short. A framework name alone is not analysis.
Calculate what matters to the question. Check units, comparisons, and assumptions. Write what each result means and what it cannot establish.
Judge alternatives by the same criteria. Explain your main trade-off, the strongest objection, and what would change your view. For a decision, identify a first action.
Record your position, supporting evidence with page or exhibit references, key calculations, and unresolved questions. Write reasons in your own words instead of copying the case.
Prepare on your own first, then meet before class when collaboration is allowed. Compare reasoning and challenge assumptions. You do not need to agree on one answer.
State your position, strongest evidence, and an important uncertainty. Be ready to explain your reasoning and ask a useful question. Avoid memorizing a speech.
Answer the question being discussed. Connect your comment to what others said. Challenge ideas respectfully and revise when warranted. Take brief notes so you can keep listening.
After class, record what changed in your thinking and why. Note a course idea you understand better, its limits, and how you could use it in another case.

footer: Independent handout by Kamyar Goudarzi, based on this exercise and William Ellet, The Case Study Handbook: A Student's Guide, revised edition, Harvard Business Review Press, 2018, chapters 3 and 7. Not a Harvard publication.
